description: Bebe Rexha rebuilds Faithless' 1995 club classic 'Insomnia' into a 2026 dance anthem about music as salvation — the lead single from Dirty Blonde, her first album as an independent artist.

pops.text: Released March 6, 2026 through Empire. It was the lead single from Dirty Blonde and Rexha's first big move after leaving Warner Records to go independent.
The track is built around Faithless' 1995 anthem 'Insomnia' — it interpolates the melody and keeps the late Maxi Jazz's famous refrain, 'I can't get no sleep.'
Faithless had said no to 'Insomnia' sample requests for roughly 30 years. Sister Bliss said Rexha was the exception — a real pop star with a plan to introduce it to a younger generation.
Rexha first heard 'Insomnia' as a kid growing up in New York, through her uncle — who was trying to become a DJ at the time.
The original was made in producer Rollo's garden-shed studio. Maxi Jazz wrote its lyric in under an hour, kept awake by a painful tooth abscess — insomnia with a dental cause.
Rexha calls this her 'love letter to music' — her sanctuary through a rough stretch of label battles and breakups. The dance floor as church, hence the title.
The song originally had no bridge. Fans kept demanding bridges in her music, so Rexha wrote one herself — and a preview of it started taking off online.
The official visual splices footage from the original 1995 'Insomnia' video with new nightclub scenes of Rexha in oversized sunglasses and layered cross pendants.
It topped Billboard's Dance/Mix Show Airplay chart in May 2026 — Rexha's fourth No. 1 there, but Faithless' first. It also went Top 10 in Germany and Belgium.

She performed it live for the first time on Jimmy Kimmel Live! just days after release, and it later earned a 2026 MTV VMA nomination for Best Dance — her first major nomination as an independent artist.

title: New Religion

description: The Bee Gees' slinky centerpiece of the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack, dreamed up in a French château before the brothers had even seen the script — it ruled No. 1 for eight weeks in 1978.

pops.text: Written for a film the brothers barely knew. Producer Robert Stigwood's brief was basically: a paint-store clerk blows his wages dancing on Saturday night. The Gibbs took it from there.

The film's working title was just 'Saturday Night' — the Bee Gees disliked it, and since they already had a song called 'Night Fever,' they talked Stigwood into retitling the movie Saturday Night Fever.
That string intro started with keyboardist Blue Weaver noodling on Percy Faith's 'Theme from A Summer Place.' Barry Gibb overheard it, insisted it was something new, and sang the riff over it.
Barry, Robin and Maurice finished the lyrics sitting on a staircase — the same way they'd written their first international hit, 'New York Mining Disaster 1941,' back in 1967.
Recording began in April 1977 at the Château d'Hérouville in France and wrapped that September in Miami. Listen closely and you'll hear a thunder sound effect shaken into the track for extra drama.
Chart rocket: it debuted at No. 76 on the Hot 100, then leapt 44 places to No. 32 in a single week, on its way up 32–17–8–5–2–1.
Eight weeks at No. 1 — the longest reign of any single in 1978. For the first five of those weeks, 'Stayin' Alive' sat right beneath it at No. 2.
One week in March 1978, songs written by Barry Gibb held four of the top five spots on the Hot 100 — with 'Night Fever' sitting on top of the pile.
Family business: 'Night Fever' replaced younger brother Andy Gibb's 'Love Is Thicker Than Water' at No. 1, and was itself replaced by Yvonne Elliman's Gibb-written 'If I Can't Have You.'

A video was shot in 1978 but not shown to the public until 2004 — the brothers in a dark studio, layered over a drive down Collins Avenue's 'Motel Row' in Miami. Most of those motels are now closed or demolished.

title: Night Fever

description: Berlin's first Top 40 hit — a Giorgio Moroder-produced synth-rock breakup song from Love Life (1984), with Terri Nunn torn between leaving and staying, and a Bonnie and Clyde video to match.

pops.text: Lead single from Love Life, released February 27, 1984. It was recorded in November 1983 at Oasis Studios in North Hollywood.
Written by bassist John Crawford, Berlin's founder and main songwriter. Terri Nunn is the voice out front, but Crawford was the band's pen.
Crawford described the lyric as two people who love each other, where one wants to end it — and neither knows how to quit without hurting the other.
Produced by Giorgio Moroder and Richie Zito. Moroder only produced two tracks on Love Life — this one and 'Dancing in Berlin'; Mike Howlett handled most of the rest of the album.
Berlin's first Top 40 entry: it peaked at No. 23 on the Billboard Hot 100 on May 12, 1984, and also reached No. 25 on the Mainstream Rock chart.
It climbed even higher overseas — No. 5 in New Zealand, and No. 23 in Australia. The paired 12-inch with 'Dancing in Berlin' reached No. 6 on Billboard's Dance Club chart.

The video casts the band as a bank-robbing gang in a Bonnie and Clyde-style car chase and shoot-out. Directed by Evan English and Paul Goldman, it was included on the Berlin Video 45 compilation in 1984.
Movie afterlife: the song turned up in the 1985 film Vision Quest, the wrestling drama starring Matthew Modine.
In 1985 it was re-released in the US as the B-side of Madonna's 'Crazy for You,' also from Vision Quest. Its own original B-side was 'Rumor of Love.'
The Moroder connection paid off big two years later: Berlin topped charts worldwide with his 'Take My Breath Away' from Top Gun in 1986.

title: No More Words

description: The signature single from Scottish band Big Country's debut album The Crossing (1983) — Stuart Adamson's bagpipe-guitar anthem about holding onto your dreams, and the band's only US Top 40 hit.

pops.text: Released in May 1983 as the third single from debut album The Crossing, produced by Steve Lillywhite — fresh off shaping U2's early sound.
Those are not bagpipes. Stuart Adamson's MXR pitch transposer pushed his guitar notes up an octave, creating that shrill, skirling, bagpipe-like whine.
Adamson also used an E-Bow, a little device that vibrates the strings magnetically for infinite sustain — part of how those guitar lines seem to float over the hills.

Credited to all four members: Adamson, Bruce Watson, Tony Butler and Mark Brzezicki. Adamson came from punk band the Skids; Watson had been working as a submarine cleaner at the Rosyth naval base when they formed the band in Dunfermline in 1981.
Neat symmetry on the charts: No. 17 in the UK and No. 17 on the Billboard Hot 100 — plus No. 3 on the US Rock Top Tracks chart and No. 3 in Canada.
The Crossing reached No. 3 in the UK and No. 18 in the US, going platinum in the UK and Canada and gold in America. This song remains Big Country's only US Top 40 single.
The video got heavy MTV rotation. The treasure hunt opens at the then-derelict Corfe Castle railway station in Dorset, the castle ruins looming behind the band. It was directed by Lindsey Clennell.
Second half, Swanage Bay: the band suits up to dive for treasure — but nobody in the band was actually scuba-certified, so the great underwater search had to stay on the surface.
The Crossing earned two Grammy nominations, Rolling Stone's year-end poll named them Best New Group, and the band played this song on Saturday Night Live in December 1983.
The Smashing Pumpkins' James Iha put it on his 'mixtape for dreamers,' saying: 'The music is super-anthemic, the guitars are awesome and bagpipe-like… it sounds like Braveheart or something.'

title: In A Big Country

artist: Big Head Todd and The Monsters
description: Big Head Todd and the Monsters' signature song — a six-minute blues-rock slow burn from the platinum Sister Sweetly (1993) that became a rock-radio staple without the help of a music video.

pops.text: Written entirely by frontman Todd Park Mohr. On Sister Sweetly it closes in as track nine, stretching out to 6 minutes 16 seconds — no radio-edit hurry here.
It wasn't new in 1993: an earlier version appeared on the band's independent 1990 album Midnight Radio. New label Giant Records wanted their best song re-recorded properly.
Sister Sweetly was the band's major-label debut, produced by David Z — best known as a Prince associate. Quite a polish-up for a Colorado bar band.
Mohr refused to make a music video for the song, right when MTV could make a career. He wanted to be a storyteller, not a video band — so there is no official clip, just the music.
Radio didn't care about the missing video: 'Bittersweet' reached No. 14 on Billboard's Mainstream Rock chart in 1993.
Sister Sweetly peaked at only No. 117 on the Billboard 200, but it refused to leave — charting for over a year, topping the Heatseekers chart, and eventually going platinum.
Band roots: Mohr, drummer Brian Nevin and bassist Rob Squires all attended Columbine High School together. Their first gig was in 1986, at a University of Colorado college party.
Before the platinum record, they were road dogs — touring the Mountain States and West Coast in a van they dubbed 'The Colonel,' racking up more than 400,000 miles.
One of three Sister Sweetly singles to crack the rock charts, alongside 'Broken Hearted Savior' (No. 9) and 'Circle' (No. 21).
It is still the emotional centerpiece of their live show — a version recorded on their 40th-anniversary tour anchors the 2025 live album 40 Live.

title: Bittersweet

description: Withers tells his friends to mind their own business over an unstoppable clavinet groove: if it feels this good getting used, keep on using him. From Still Bill, it stopped one spot short of No. 1.

pops.text: Album two: this is from Still Bill, Withers' second album, released in 1972 on Sussex Records — the follow-up that also gave the world 'Lean on Me.'
It arrived as a single in August 1972, after 'Lean on Me' had topped the charts, with 'Let Me in Your Life' tucked on the B-side.
Origin story, in Withers' own telling: women kept telling him he was 'too nice,' and he wrote this playful, arrogant reply while working at McDonnell Douglas in Long Beach.
That nagging, chattering hook is Ray Jackson on clavinet. Critic Robert Christgau singled Jackson out for furnishing 'the hook of the year' on this song.
The band behind him came from Charles Wright's Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band: James Gadson on drums, Melvin Dunlap on bass and Benorce Blackmon on guitar.
So close: it peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, kept out of the top spot by Michael Jackson's 'Ben' and Chuck Berry's 'My Ding-a-Ling.' It also hit No. 2 on the soul chart.
Withers performed it on Soul Train on November 4, 1972. Billboard ranked it the No. 78 song of 1972, and the single was certified Gold by the RIAA.
Christgau's verdict: he called 'Use Me' one of the few knowledgeable songs about sex that supposedly sexy pop music had ever produced.
Grace Jones remade it with a reggae-influenced arrangement on her 1981 album Nightclubbing, then released her version as a single, too.
The groove kept working: UGK sampled it for 'Use Me Up' in 1992, and Kendrick Lamar sampled its recurring drum break on 'Sing About Me, I'm Dying of Thirst' in 2012.

title: Use Me

description: A wordless funk jam Preston improvised on clavinet through a wah-wah pedal — buried as a B-side, flipped by DJs, and flown all the way to No. 2 and a Grammy.

pops.text: This instrumental first appeared on I Wrote a Simple Song, Preston's 1971 debut album for A&M Records, after he left the Beatles' Apple label.
The sound is a trick: Preston ran a clavinet through a wah-wah pedal, a pairing that helped popularize the clavinet's funky bite in the 1970s.
No chart, no plan: Preston improvised the groove in the studio while calling out chord changes to the backing band, then added organ and hand claps on top.
He named it 'Outa-Space' simply because the finished instrumental sounded spacy to him. Preston co-wrote it with Joe Greene and produced it himself.
Check the personnel: George Harrison plays guitar and Dobro on the track, alongside guitarist David T. Walker and percussionist King Errisson on congas.
A&M did not believe in it: the label issued it as the B-side of 'I Wrote a Simple Song' on December 20, 1971. Radio DJs started flipping the single over anyway.
The flip won. The A-side stalled at No. 77 on the Hot 100, while 'Outa-Space' climbed to No. 2 — held off No. 1 by Bill Withers' 'Lean on Me,' which it succeeded atop the R&B chart.
It sold over a million copies and was awarded a Gold disc by the RIAA in June 1972. In Britain it was more modest, peaking at No. 44 late in 1972.
Award hardware: 'Outa-Space' won the Grammy Award for Best Pop Instrumental Performance for 1972, presented at the 1973 Grammys.
Afterlife: Preston performed a vocal version retitled 'All Spaced Out' on The Midnight Special in 1973, and in the 1990s Intel used the original to promote its MMX Pentium processors.

title: Outa-Space

description: An Austin busker's rooftop song becomes a psychedelic-soul anthem about mortality and togetherness — and lands Record of the Year and inauguration stages.

pops.text: Third single, first phenomenon: it was released on April 16, 2019, ahead of the duo's self-titled debut album, which followed on June 21, 2019, on ATO Records.
Split duties: singer Eric Burton wrote the song alone, and guitarist Adrian Quesada produced it. Burton sings lead; Quesada built the track around him.
Burton started it as a beginner: he has said he wrote it while learning guitar, after waking from a nap on his uncle's rooftop in Alamogordo, New Mexico, playing whatever notes sounded good.

Its spark was the multicolored tones of the sky, and its themes are mortality and togetherness. Burton was leading worship at a church at the time, which explains the gospel singers lifting the chorus.
Unlikely pairing: Burton had been busking — on Santa Monica Pier, then on Austin streets — when he was connected with Quesada, a veteran of Latin funk band Grupo Fantasma, in 2017.
On the album it sits at track two and runs 4:06, filed under psychedelic soul with blues and funk in its DNA.
Radio slow-burn: it topped Billboard's Adult Alternative Airplay chart for a week in February 2020, nearly a year after release, and peaked at No. 21 on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs.
The official video arrived November 22, 2019, directed by Kristian Mercado and shot entirely in the Bronx, celebrating family, movement and life there.

Grammy sweep: at the 2021 Grammys, 'Colors' was nominated for Record of the Year and Best American Roots Performance, the deluxe album was up for Album of the Year, and the duo performed the song on the show.

From busking to the inauguration: Black Pumas performed 'Colors' for Celebrating America, the primetime special on the night of President Biden's inauguration in January 2021. The single is now RIAA Platinum in the US.

title: Colors

description: Jack Antonoff and Lorde turn a private mantra — don't sell out, stay and fight for the relationship — into a huge, Springsteen-sized synth-pop lead single for Gone Now.

pops.text: Lead single duty: released March 30, 2017, by RCA as the first single from Bleachers' second album, Gone Now, where it sits as track four.
Late-night write: Antonoff co-wrote it with Lorde, credited under her birth name, Ella Yelich-O'Connor, in a late-night studio session — then spent a year twisting the track around.
Listen to the last chorus: Lorde is in there, singing uncredited backing vocals behind Antonoff.
Production bench: Antonoff produced it with Greg Kurstin and Vince Clarke — Clarke of Depeche Mode, Yazoo and Erasure fame — plus Kurstin on LinnDrum and keyboards.
Not about cash: Antonoff says the title is a phrase he repeats to himself as motivation. In his words to Newsweek, it means 'don't sell out' — a lover staying despite the relationship's misfortunes.
Antonoff has said the song was inspired by Lena Dunham, his girlfriend at the time. She later directed its music video.
Drum genealogy: Antonoff told Vulture that the Linn drums from Queen's 1984 hit 'Radio Ga Ga' inspired this track's percussion.
Treasure hunt launch: the day before release, Antonoff hid flash drives containing the song inside piñatas shaped like himself in Manhattan's Union Square, bats included.
Chart run: No. 3 on Billboard's Alternative Songs, No. 15 on Rock Airplay and No. 22 on Adult Pop Songs — and the single was later certified Gold by the RIAA.
The Dunham video, shot in New Jersey and released May 2, 2017, casts Antonoff as a groom, Alia Shawkat as the officiant, and twin models Giulia and Camilla Venturini as bride and her lover.

title: Don't Take The Money

description: Steve Winwood, just 21, sings the quiet center of Blind Faith's only album — a folk-rock prayer from a supergroup that burned out within a single year.

pops.text: Supergroup roll call: Blind Faith united Eric Clapton and Ginger Baker from Cream, Steve Winwood from Traffic and Ric Grech from Family.
One and done: this comes from the band's self-titled debut, released in August 1969 — the only studio album Blind Faith ever made. The song is track two of six.
Winwood wrote it alone, and he was 21 or younger when he did: born in May 1948, he had only just turned 21 when the album came out.
It was recorded in London in spring 1969 with producer Jimmy Miller, and runs a tight 3:16 — a folk-rock ballad amid the album's blues-rock muscle.
Personnel: Winwood sings and plays guitars and keyboards, Clapton plays guitar, Grech plays bass, and Baker handles drums and percussion.
Do not ask him what it means: Winwood has never explained the song publicly, saying explaining a song is like telling a joke and then having to explain it.
Rolling Stone's original album review praised Ginger Baker's 'highly innovative percussion' on this song and called its signature wasted-and-lost lyric 'delightful.'
Huge before they had barely played: the band's live debut was a free Hyde Park concert on June 7, 1969, before an estimated 100,000 people — and the album went to No. 1 in both the US and UK.
Odd single life: in 1969 it was only a B-side in some countries, including on the Australian release of 'Well All Right.' The US finally got it as an A-side on RSO in 1977.
Clapton kept it alive after the band split within the year: on his 1976 and 1977 tours, he had singer Yvonne Elliman sing 'Can't Find My Way Home' in the show.

title: Can't Find My Way Home

description: Blind Melon's sunny-sounding signature song — a depression lyric in a major key, carried to fame by Samuel Bayer's 'Bee Girl' video. It topped the rock charts and turned a slow-selling debut album multi-platinum.

pops.text: It sits on the band's self-titled debut album, released September 22, 1992 on Capitol — nearly a year before the single took off in 1993.
Bassist Brad Smith wrote most of it before Blind Melon even existed, though like the rest of the album it is credited to the whole band.
Smith has said the song came from watching a girlfriend struggle with depression: it is about not being able to get out of bed and find a reason to face the day.
The debut was recorded at London Bridge Studio in Seattle with producer Rick Parashar, largely live with minimal overdubs.
Director Samuel Bayer — fresh off Nirvana's 'Smells Like Teen Spirit' — built the video around a tap-dancing 'Bee Girl' and MTV put it in heavy rotation.
Bee Girl was 10-year-old Heather DeLoach, the first girl to audition. She was cast because she resembled the album cover's bee-costumed child.
That cover photo, shot in 1975, shows Georgia Graham — younger sister of drummer Glenn Graham — in her own dance-recital bee costume.
Chart peak: No. 20 on the Billboard Hot 100, but No. 1 on both the Album Rock Tracks and Modern Rock Tracks charts — and No. 1 in Canada.

The Bee Girl escaped the video: DeLoach reprised the role in 'Weird Al' Yankovic's 'Bedrock Anthem' video, and Chris Farley played her when Blind Melon performed on Saturday Night Live in January 1994.
An early alternate take, the 'Ripped Away' version with different music and Hoon singing the original lyrics, surfaced on the band's 1996 odds-and-ends collection Nico.

title: No Rain

description: Darin's swinging remake of a French standard: Charles Trenet's 'La Mer' reborn as an American love song. The follow-up to 'Mack the Knife,' it proved the teen idol could out-swing the crooners — and hit No. 6.

pops.text: Before it was Darin's, it was French: the melody is Charles Trenet's 'La Mer,' written in 1943 and published in 1946 as an ode to the sea itself.
American songwriter Jack Lawrence wrote the English lyrics in 1946 — not a translation, but a new story about lovers separated by an ocean.
The English version had been around for years before Darin: Benny Goodman was among the artists who recorded 'Beyond the Sea' in the 1940s.
Darin recorded it for That's All, his second album — a deliberate leap from teen-idol rock and roll into big-band standards, arranged by Richard Wess.
Lawrence later recalled giving the young Darin a copy of the song; Darin said he liked earlier versions but felt the song lacked a definite beat. His recording fixed that.
That's All was released in March 1959 and spent 52 weeks on Billboard's album chart, peaking at No. 7.
Released as a single on Atco in January 1960, with 'That's the Way Love Is' on the B-side, it was the follow-up to the No. 1 smash 'Mack the Knife.'
It reached No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 15 on the US R&B chart and No. 7 in Canada in early 1960.
That breakout year ended at the second Grammy Awards, where Darin won Record of the Year — for 'Mack the Knife' — and Best New Artist.
The song became Darin's signature — so much so that Kevin Spacey's 2004 film biography of Darin was titled Beyond the Sea, with Spacey doing his own singing.

title: Beyond the Sea

description: A million-selling Muscle Shoals soul single from a Montgomery club band: Bobby Moore wrote it, Chico Jenkins sang it, and Chess Records took the FAME Studios tape national — No. 27 pop, No. 7 R&B in 1966.

pops.text: Bandleader Bobby Moore was a New Orleans-born tenor saxophonist. He formed the first Rhythm Aces in 1952, while stationed with the US Army at Fort Benning, Georgia.
Moore rebuilt the band after moving to Montgomery, Alabama in 1961, adding his brother Larry on alto sax and vocalist-guitarist Chico Jenkins.
The Montgomery lineup earned its living on the club circuit and backed visiting stars including Sam Cooke and Ray Charles.
Moore wrote 'Searching For My Love' himself — but he doesn't sing it. The lead vocal is Chico Jenkins, a detail many listeners got wrong because the label never said so.
The group cut the song in late 1965 at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama — the studio then building its legend in Southern soul.
They were the first act on Chicago's Chess Records to record at FAME. Leonard and Marshall Chess heard the tape, bought the rights and released it on their Checker label.
Its success changed Chess's map: the label began booking its other artists time at FAME, most notably Etta James.
The single entered the Billboard Hot 100 on June 25, 1966 at No. 88 and climbed for ten weeks on the chart.
Peak numbers: No. 27 on the Hot 100 on August 13, 1966, and No. 7 on the R&B chart — while in Los Angeles it hit No. 1 on the leading pop and soul stations.
It sold more than a million copies. The soundalike follow-up, 'Try My Love Again,' could only manage No. 97 — the band never repeated this hit.

title: Searching For My Love

description: Jason Bonham — son of Led Zeppelin's John Bonham — steps out with his own band's debut hit: a Zeppelin-tinged rocker produced by Bob Ezrin that hit No. 9 on the rock chart and sent the album gold.

pops.text: The drummer is Jason Bonham, son of Led Zeppelin's John Bonham. Jason started on drums at age four and appeared on a scaled-down kit in Zeppelin's film The Song Remains the Same.
In May 1988 he sat in his father's place, playing with the three surviving members of Led Zeppelin at the Atlantic Records 40th Anniversary concert.
He also drummed on Jimmy Page's 1988 solo album Outrider and toured behind it before forming his own band, Bonham, in 1989.
'Wait for You' is track two on the band's debut album, The Disregard of Timekeeping, released in 1989, and runs 5:02.
The lineup: Canadian singer Daniel MacMaster, guitarist Ian Hatton and bassist-keyboardist John Smithson alongside Bonham.
All five share the songwriting credit — Bonham, MacMaster, Hatton and Smithson, plus producer Bob Ezrin, the man behind albums by Alice Cooper and Pink Floyd.
Rock radio carried it: the single spent 22 weeks on Billboard's Album Rock Tracks chart and peaked at No. 9 in November 1989.
On the Hot 100 it was slower going — it debuted at No. 91 in late November 1989 and climbed to a No. 55 peak seven weeks later.
The album outperformed the single, reaching No. 38 on Billboard's album chart and earning Bonham a gold record.
It remains the band's only Hot 100 entry. After one more album, Mad Hatter in 1992, Bonham split, and Jason moved on to session work and other bands.

title: Wait for You

artist: Bonny Light Horseman, Eric D. Johnson, Josh Kaufman, Anaïs Mitchell
description: A one-take, wee-hours folk song from the trio of Anaïs Mitchell, Fruit Bats' Eric D. Johnson and producer Josh Kaufman — a brand-new song that accidentally echoes the centuries-old 'The Water Is Wide.'

pops.text: Bonny Light Horseman is a trio: singer-songwriter Anaïs Mitchell, Eric D. Johnson of Fruit Bats, and multi-instrumentalist-producer Josh Kaufman.
The group came together after Justin Vernon and Aaron Dessner invited them to perform at the 2018 Eaux Claires festival in Wisconsin.
'Deep In Love' began as a Fruit Bats sketch — Johnson's own song — before it found its way into the trio's traditional-leaning repertoire.
Kaufman spotted what Johnson hadn't planned: the sketch closely resembled a traditional tune of the same name, sharing lyrics with 'Waly Waly,' better known as 'The Water Is Wide.'
What you hear is the first and only take, recorded in the wee hours of a midwinter night at Dreamland Studio in Woodstock, New York.
Johnson sings the lead, including the seafaring image at its heart: a ship that sailed as deep as it could be — but not so deep in love as the singer.
It was released in October 2019 as the second single from the trio's debut, following the title track, 'Bonny Light Horseman.'
On the album it is track two of ten and, at just over five minutes, the longest song on the record.
The self-titled album, produced by Kaufman, arrived January 24, 2020 on 37d03d Records — the label collective founded by Vernon and Dessner.
The album was recorded in two places: The Funkhaus in Berlin and Dreamland in upstate New York, with guests including Vernon, Dessner and Lisa Hannigan.

title: Deep In Love
